Unix timestamps: seconds vs milliseconds

A numeric timestamp needs a unit. Interpreting seconds as milliseconds can move a modern date into 1970; interpreting milliseconds as seconds can send it far into the future. Start with the source’s contract, then check the conversion.

By ParseCove · Published 27 November 2026

On this pageCheck the unitCompare interpretationsJavaScript & PythonUTC and time zonesTroubleshootingTerms & FAQ

Seconds and milliseconds can describe the same instant

The Unix epoch is 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z. Unix timestamps conventionally use seconds; some APIs and libraries represent an epoch timestamp in milliseconds. Multiply seconds by 1,000 to obtain milliseconds. Dividing milliseconds by 1,000 can produce a fractional number of seconds.

milliseconds = seconds × 1,000
One instant, with its unit included
RepresentationValue
Seconds1700000000
Milliseconds1700000000000
ISO date in UTC2023-11-14T22:13:20.000Z

Modern dates often have 10 digits in seconds and 13 in milliseconds. That is a useful clue, not a unit definition. A millisecond timestamp close to the epoch can be very short, and a far-future timestamp in seconds can be long. Check the API schema, field documentation or producing code.

References: MDN: Date and epoch milliseconds · Python: datetime.fromtimestamp.

Convert timestamp units in JavaScript and Python

The JavaScript Date constructor expects a numeric timestamp in milliseconds. Convert a known seconds value once before passing it in. Date.now() and getTime() already return milliseconds, so multiplying those values again is a unit mistake.

JavaScript: seconds, milliseconds and the 1970 mistake

const seconds = 1700000000;
const milliseconds = 1700000000000;

console.log(new Date(seconds * 1000).toISOString());
// 2023-11-14T22:13:20.000Z
console.log(new Date(milliseconds).toISOString());
// 2023-11-14T22:13:20.000Z

// Passing seconds directly treats that number as milliseconds:
console.log(new Date(seconds).toISOString());
// 1970-01-20T16:13:20.000Z

console.log(new Date(1700000000123).toISOString());
// 2023-11-14T22:13:20.123Z

Reference: MDN: Date.now returns milliseconds.

Python’s datetime.fromtimestamp() takes a timestamp in seconds. Pass an explicit timezone to obtain an aware UTC result. For integer milliseconds, the following example keeps the millisecond remainder instead of discarding it.

Python 3: UTC dates with the millisecond remainder preserved

from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

seconds = 1700000000
print(datetime.fromtimestamp(seconds, tz=timezone.utc).isoformat(timespec="milliseconds"))
# 2023-11-14T22:13:20.000+00:00

# Split integer milliseconds so the remainder is preserved, including before 1970.
for milliseconds in [1700000000123, -1]:
    whole_seconds, remainder_ms = divmod(milliseconds, 1000)
    instant = datetime.fromtimestamp(whole_seconds, tz=timezone.utc)
    instant += timedelta(milliseconds=remainder_ms)
    print(instant.isoformat(timespec="milliseconds"))
# 2023-11-14T22:13:20.123+00:00
# 1969-12-31T23:59:59.999+00:00

Keep the original integer millisecond value if you need that precision. Converting it to whole seconds and dropping the remainder loses information. Python datetime and JavaScript Date also have different supported ranges; a date accepted by one is not automatically accepted by the other.

A time zone changes the displayed date, not the unit

2023-11-14T22:13:20Z and 2023-11-15T06:13:20+08:00 describe the same instant. Both map to 1700000000000 epoch milliseconds. A different calendar day in the display does not mean the timestamp has changed.

JavaScript: two timezone-explicit dates, one timestamp

const utc = Date.parse('2023-11-14T22:13:20Z');
const offset = Date.parse('2023-11-15T06:13:20+08:00');
console.log(utc === offset);
// true
console.log(utc);
// 1700000000000

When converting a date string in the Unix timestamp converter, include Z or an explicit numeric offset. A date and time without a timezone may be ambiguous. Named time zones can also have daylight-saving rules that depend on the date.

Check these causes before changing the number

SymptomWhat to check
An expected modern date appears in 1970Seconds may have been passed to an API expecting milliseconds. Confirm the source unit before multiplying.
A date lands far in the future or exceeds the rangeMilliseconds may have been treated as seconds, or multiplied by 1,000 twice.
The date differs by several hoursCompare the displayed timezone and the original date string’s offset. A unit mismatch is a separate problem.
The last three digits disappearCheck whether a millisecond value was rounded or truncated to whole seconds.
An automatic unit choice looks wrongUse the documented input unit explicitly. Digit counts and magnitude heuristics cannot establish the original meaning.

For example, 999 milliseconds is 1970-01-01T00:00:00.999Z. The same number in seconds is 1970-01-01T00:16:39.000Z. Both are valid dates, so plausibility alone cannot identify the producer’s unit.

Terms used in this guide

Unix epoch
The reference instant at the start of 1 January 1970 in UTC.
Epoch seconds
A numeric timestamp expressed in seconds relative to the epoch. The unit is part of its meaning.
Epoch milliseconds
The corresponding millisecond representation. One second equals 1,000 milliseconds.
UTC and Z
UTC is the time reference used by the examples. A trailing Z on an ISO date indicates a zero UTC offset.

Common questions

Are all 13-digit values millisecond timestamps?

No. A digit count is only a clue for dates in a familiar range. The field could use a different unit, a far-future seconds value or an unrelated identifier. Confirm the source contract.

Why does a timestamp show a different day in another timezone?

The same instant can fall on different local calendar days. Check an explicit UTC output before deciding that the timestamp or its unit is wrong.

Can timestamps be negative?

Yes. Negative values represent instants before the epoch. -1 second and -1 millisecond are different instants, as the comparison shows.

Does the tool accept fractional seconds, microseconds or nanoseconds?

The numeric modes accept integer seconds or integer milliseconds. The ISO date mode accepts up to three fractional second digits. Microsecond and nanosecond inputs need an explicit conversion and a decision about any precision loss; this tool does not guess those units.

USE AN EXPLICIT UNIT
